characteristics: The CTA is the most important actionable element, tied to the primary goal (sales/signups). It must capture immediate attention via visual weight.
dos: Use a unique color or style that doesn't compete with other screen elements; ensure enough contrast with the background; use wording that calls to an action; hide or de-emphasize secondary actions (e.g. tuck them into a menu) so the primary CTA has no visual competition.
donts: Do not use more than one instance of a primary CTA on one page to avoid dividing user attention; do not use ghost buttons for main CTAs; don't size the CTA so small it's missed or so big it triggers banner blindness.

characteristics: Users have a pre-existing representation in their heads of how a product or system works based on past experience.
dos: Do research to understand the mental models of your target audience. Design the conceptual model to match the mental model.
donts: Don't let the conceptual model 'bubble up' from the technology/database structure.

characteristics: Users use visual design (look and feel) as the first indicator of whether to trust a site.
dos: Use professional layout, color, and font to pass the initial 'trust rejection' phase. Ensure content is credible for long-term trust.
donts: Don't neglect first impressions; users will reject a site based on poor design before even reading the content.

characteristics: Design files and shipped code must stay in exact sync - component names, spacing, and states specified in the design file should have a one-to-one equivalent in code.
dos: Ensure names in the design file (Figma or equivalent) and the code match exactly; define typography treatments and use a consistent spacing grid (e.g. an 8-pixel grid); document interactions precisely so engineering can build them without guessing.
donts: Don't let art direction and engineering get out of sync; don't allow inconsistent naming or deviations from the master design file across platforms.

characteristics: Research-driven design ensures the right product gets built for the user, not just the one that's easiest to build.
dos: Write the user problem down in one sentence before proposing any solution; conduct research, analyze usage data, and talk to real users or clients to validate that problem; structure the product so tasks can be completed quickly, using skeuomorphic or familiar cues for less tech-savvy audiences where helpful.
donts: Don't make assumptions about user requirements without grounded data; don't move to implementation before the problem is validated; don't ignore the specific demographics of the target audience.

characteristics: Familiarity with shapes associated with action improves recognition speed. Deviation increases identification time.
dos: Use rectangles or rounded rectangles as the safest choice. Ensure buttons stand out from other elements.
donts: Do not use organic or irregular shapes (triangle, circle) unless the style requires it.

characteristics: Physical size affects the ease of tapping or clicking; too-small targets lead to frustration and errors.
dos: Start with 44 x 44pt for mobile primary targets (50pt ideal; roughly 7mm x 7mm); for cursor-based devices, 32 x 32 points is acceptable; leave at least a 2mm (~8px) gap between adjacent touch targets.
donts: Do not make buttons smaller than the recommended minimum; don't place touch targets too close together, leading to accidental presses.

characteristics: Contrast ratio determines readability and accessibility for users, including those with impaired vision.
dos: Aim for at least AA contrast ratio between labels and backgrounds. Use saturation that works in light/dark modes.
donts: Do not use low contrast ratios that make buttons look like decoration; avoid high contrast that causes eye strain.

characteristics: Designing for exploration and error prevention so users never fear making a mistake.
dos: Design interactions so they are impossible to mis-tap; treat the UI like a children's toy; use warnings and confirmations before destructive actions; provide sensible default values and easy undo instead of complex confirmations; make buttons large enough to tap easily.
donts: Don't create fragile interfaces where users can easily make irreversible errors; don't let users cruise through hazardous procedures on 'autopilot'; don't place destructive actions (Delete) next to frequent, positive actions.

characteristics: Prioritizing long-term utility and accessibility over temporary design trends.
dos: Adopt technology only when it serves a proven purpose for the majority of users.
donts: Introduce stylistic features like parallax effects just for the sake of following a trend.

characteristics: Distinguishing between navigation and data manipulation.
dos: Use buttons for changing/manipulating data; use links for navigating between pages.
donts: Use primary button styles for simple navigation tasks that don't involve state changes.

characteristics: The brain can only process a small amount of information at a time; showing only what's needed avoids overwhelming users and prevents cognitive overload.
dos: Show people what they need when they need it; reveal details only as needed contextually; show only relevant context and use progressive disclosure for deeper detail.
donts: Don't give too much information all at once; don't display all content at once if it isn't necessary for the immediate task; don't worry about counting clicks if they reduce cognitive load.

characteristics: Different demands use different mental resources. Cognitive load is the most expensive.
dos: Minimize cognitive load even if it increases motor load (clicks). Ensure targets are large enough (Fitt's Law).
donts: Don't make people think or remember more than necessary. Don't make targets too small or far apart.

characteristics: Time is relative; mental processing and expectations influence frustration.
dos: Always provide progress indicators (skeleton screens, average-color blocks). Keep task time consistent.
donts: Don't make users wait without feedback; don't use empty white screens or center-page spinners only.

characteristics: Providing instant responses to user actions even while background validations occur to reduce perceived latency.
dos: Register an action instantly in the UI while syncing in the background.
donts: Do not show a loading spinner for every minor interaction; don't make users wait for complex checks.

characteristics: Optimal timing changes based on viewport size and element complexity.
dos: Use 100-200ms for small components; 500-700ms for page transitions.
donts: Don't make users 'watch the clock' by using slow progress indicators or spinners.

principle: Text needs consistent contrast on images
characteristics: Background images are dynamic and can make overlaid text unreadable, especially in hero sections.
dos: Add a semi-transparent overlay (dark for light text); lower image contrast; add a soft text shadow or large-blur-radius shadow to increase legibility.
donts: Don't place text directly on a busy image without a contrast-improving treatment; don't slap a headline over a raw hero image without checking contrast across both light and dark areas of the image.

characteristics: Design decisions should account for target audience demographics and physical context - the platform and environment change usage variables.
dos: Account for viewing distance, indoor/outdoor use, and input methods (e.g. remote for TV, thumb for mobile); adjust text size and contrast for the specific environment.
donts: Don't ignore the suitability of the interface style for the target age group; don't apply mobile variables to TV; don't design for TV the same way you design for a mobile phone.

characteristics: Link and control text must make sense on its own, including to screen-reader users who navigate by jumping between links.
dos: Write descriptive link text that states the destination or action (e.g. 'Download the pricing PDF'); build accessibility into the process from the start.
donts: Don't use vague link text like 'Click here' or 'Read more' with no context; don't rely on surrounding text alone to make a link's purpose clear.

characteristics: Maintaining predictable behavior and layout across multiple screens.
dos: Keep margins and placement of common items (title bars, back buttons) the same; use grids.
donts: Don't allow objects to 'jump around' between different views of the interface.

characteristics: Making the overall experience feel like one coherent service across multiple devices and touchpoints, minimizing the reorientation a person feels when moving between them.
dos: Specify which functionality belongs on each device; create guidelines that span multiple device types; design for coherency across all touchpoints so users don't have to re-learn navigation.
donts: Don't treat devices as isolated cells; avoid disjointed UIs; don't force users to re-learn navigation on every page or provide inconsistent experiences across channels (web/phone).

characteristics: Interfaces depend on visual representation of objects, physical actions instead of syntax, and rapid, reversible, immediately visible effects.
dos: Ensure interface actions are aligned with user understanding; provide immediate feedback; allow actions to be reversed.
donts: Don't distance the user from the consequences of their actions; don't use complex syntax or force users into logical conditions for simple tasks.

characteristics: Allowing users to experience benefits before requiring investment of effort or data.
dos: Let users engage with core features before asking them to sign up; prompt for sign-in during task saving.
donts: Don't use 'Sign up' and 'Sign in' together as the terms are confusingly similar.

principle: Feature Broad Range of Types on Homepage
characteristics: First-time users rely on homepage visuals to infer the site's product catalog and breadth. Narrow selections lead to misinterpretation.
dos: Ensure a broad selection of different product types are featured; use images or thumbnails; dedicate space to non-popular categories.
donts: Only feature a small selection of product types; assume users will know the site sells other items.

principle: Filters vs. Categories for Shared Attributes
characteristics: Wrongly implementing filters as categories prevents users from mixing criteria (e.g., 'mummy' + 'down' sleeping bag).
dos: Use categories for mutually exclusive hierarchy scopes; use filters for attributes where multiple can be selected.
donts: Implement product type as a category if attributes are the same across types; use brand-based categories.

characteristics: Redundancy makes it difficult to know which option to select and makes the site look unprofessional.
dos: Manually create the taxonomy; map manufacturer data to your own curated categories; check for combined categories.
donts: Use auto-generated categorization; reuse manufacturer categories without merging across vendors.

characteristics: Users struggle to find and verify compatibility (e.g. laptop chargers). Completion rates are very low without explicit cross-linking.
dos: Create unique pages for each compatibility product; include series-level pages; link these in cross-sell sections.
donts: Assume users know their model's specific specs; force users to manually compare dimensions from different pages.

principle: Avoid Relying Solely on Thematic Categories
characteristics: Users expect a site to be structured by 'type of product.' Purely thematic navigation breaks mental models.
dos: Use thematic paths as secondary options; ensure the core navigation is based on product types.
donts: Replace product type categories with brand or occasion categories entirely.

principle: Main Nav Categories as First Hierarchy Level
characteristics: Hiding categories behind a singular "Products" link causes double-hover issues and prevents inferring site type at a glance.
dos: Place top-level categories permanently in the main navigation bar; use non-product categories (e.g. "Deals") alongside them.
donts: Scope the entire catalog within a solitary "Products" item; use double-hover activation areas with short heights.

characteristics: Non-product links (Contact, Sign-in, Shipping) clutter the header but are vital for those who need them.
dos: Use white space or background colors to separate courtesy links; group them into sections; include a 'Shipping' link.
donts: Place courtesy navigation below primary product navigation; omit vital policy links from the header entirely.

principle: Have First 1-2 Levels as Sub-Category Pages
characteristics: Sub-category pages act as storefronts, clearing up ambiguity via thumbnails and descriptions before showing products.
dos: Display sub-categories high on the page; include thumbnails; provide a "View All" option for each scope.
donts: Display a product list for broad categories; push sub-category links below the fold with featured products.

principle: Avoid Dividing or Sub-Dividing Product Lists
characteristics: Thematic divisions make lists hard to sort and can lead users to think they've reached the end of results prematurely.
dos: Use product type filters instead of sectional dividers; show a single continuous list of products.
donts: Divide lists into thematic sections on one page; use product sliders or tabs to sub-divide featured results.

characteristics: Comforting screens that occur when things go wrong without destroying user data.
dos: Keep all user input safe; provide a clear path to resolution and use human, positive language.
donts: Do not use 'Blue Screen of Death' style jargon; never delete user work due to a form error.

characteristics: Most users hold phones one-handed with the thumb anchored at the bottom; primary controls should sit within its natural sweeping arc.
dos: Place primary actions and navigation near the bottom of the screen for large mobile devices; use bottom tab menus for high accessibility; design for a natural sweeping thumb arc.
donts: Avoid placing critical navigation (like 'Back' or 'Purchase') in the top-left 'Ow' zone; don't place primary navigation in top corners (like hamburger menus), which are the least accessible for one-handed use; don't assume users will change their grip to reach controls.

characteristics: Reducing the work required of the user beyond their initial, informed consent.
dos: Use intelligent defaults and automate repeated actions only after initial informed consent is obtained.
donts: Don't use behind-the-scenes trickery to act on the user's behalf; don't automate any action the user hasn't consented to first.

characteristics: Readability is affected by existing knowledge, titles, and text structure.
dos: Provide meaningful titles and headlines; use simple words and shorter syllables.
donts: Assume people will remember specific information just because they read it.

characteristics: Working memory is fragile and easily disrupted by sensory input.
dos: Keep information in one place so users don't have to remember it across pages.
donts: Ask users to do another task while holding information in working memory.

principle: People remember only a handful of items at once
characteristics: Working memory is limited; a widely cited guideline puts it at 4+/-1 items (sometimes cited as 7+/-2) - treat it as a working-memory guideline, not a hard law.
dos: Chunk information aggressively into small groups (roughly 3-5 items); keep information in one place so users don't have to hold it in memory across pages.
donts: Don't list many items in a single ungrouped block without further categorization; don't require users to remember information while performing another task.

principle: People are more motivated as they get closer to a goal
characteristics: The goal-gradient effect states that behavior accelerates as the goal comes into sight.
dos: Show progress bars; provide an 'illusion of progress' (e.g., a 10-stamp card with 2 pre-filled).
donts: Ignore the post-reward resetting phenomenon where motivation drops after a goal is met.

characteristics: Humans 'satisfice,' meaning they look for the good-enough solution rather than the optimal one.
dos: Design for scanning; use white space and large fonts to make a task look 'easy'.
donts: Provide too many options that require heavy analysis.

characteristics: Users typically scan digital content in an F-shaped pattern - top to bottom along the left edge - so button placement should follow that natural scanning path to keep the flow to checkout moving.
dos: Place buttons below descriptive elements; align buttons and calls-to-action along the left edge or bottom of descriptive content, following the F-pattern (top to bottom, left edge).
donts: Do not place the strongest visual element in the middle of a scan path or a position that forces the eyes to travel back and forth excessively, which slows processing.

characteristics: Clarity and efficiency always precede aesthetic concerns in the priority hierarchy.
dos: Ensure a product's title, price, and key specs are fully legible even if it requires a less 'perfect' layout - e.g. let a long product name wrap to a second line rather than truncating the size or color that distinguishes it.
donts: Don't clip or hide important content (like a product's distinguishing variant or price) just to maintain a clean visual look in a search results grid.

characteristics: Creates a sense of efficiency and responsiveness while remaining subtle.
dos: Use for micro-interactions like button states, dropdowns, and data table rendering.
donts: Do not use dramatic or slow animations in task-heavy productivity contexts.

characteristics: Entrances should inform exits to establish spatial orientation.
dos: Animate objects back to their origin point (e.g., if it entered from bottom, exit to bottom).
donts: Do not have objects disappear in a direction unrelated to their entry, which confuses the user's mental map.

characteristics: The 'zenith' of the product's potential with maximum value and content.
dos: Start design with the ideal state to set the tone for all other states.
donts: Do not design empty or error states without first defining the ideal functional state.

characteristics: Designing for 'smart but busy' users who want to complete a task quickly without feeling like a novice.
dos: Use clear text labels on controls and icons whenever a control's meaning isn't universally obvious; focus on helping 'intermediate' users get the task done fast.
donts: Don't force users to memorize abstract, unlabeled icons; don't ship an icon-only control for an uncommon action without a text label or tooltip.

characteristics: Reducing clutter by removing redundant labels when formats or context are clear.
dos: Use formatting (like $ or @) to imply the nature of data; combine labels into values (e.g., '12 left in stock').
donts: Don't use a 'label: value' format as a default; it gives equal emphasis to all data and creates noise.

characteristics: The state seen when there is no data to show (first use, cleared data, or no search results) is an opportunity for engagement, not a dead end.
dos: Tell the user exactly which button to press and why; incorporate illustrations and clear calls-to-action (e.g. 'Add First Item'); use stand-in content to show potential.
donts: Don't settle for 'No items found' or 'Nothing to see here' text with no path forward; don't use oppressive 'coach marks' that cover the UI.

characteristics: Ensuring the product doesn't break under real-world data stress.
dos: Check designs with long blocks of text, translations, and missing or varied images.
donts: Do not only design for 'best-case' or pretty artwork that will break in production.

characteristics: Text must be comfortable to read on digital screens; most information is conveyed through text, so size, leading, and line length all matter, and x-height affects perceived size.
dos: Use at least 12pt font (16pt/1em preferred, in a typeface with a large x-height); set line spacing (leading) to at least 1.5x the font size; keep line lengths between 45-75 characters; provide meaningful titles and headlines with simple words and shorter syllables.
donts: Avoid serif fonts for visually impaired users; don't use all-caps for long paragraphs; don't use moving or blinking text; don't accept default font settings without checking size, leading, and line length; don't assume people will remember specific information just because they read it once.

characteristics: Confirming user actions through visual or auditory cues.
dos: Use spinners or progress messages for loading states; use pressed states for buttons; provide feedback in multiple forms (visual + sound).
donts: Do not leave a user wondering if an app has frozen during processing.

principle: Which Attributes to Include in the List Item
characteristics: Providing enough info to decide whether to skip or explore a product.
dos: Include price, thumbnail, title/type, variations, and user ratings; add 1-3 category-specific attributes (e.g., dimensions for bags).
donts: Overload the list item with too much information; use a 'one size fits all' attribute set for all categories.

principle: Product Variations as One or Multiple List Items
characteristics: Strategy for displaying color, size, or material versions of a single product.
dos: Combine variations into a single list item for minor or non-visual differences; display separate list items for meaningful visual differences (patterns, textures).
donts: Clutter the list by showing every size or format as a separate item; fail to link variations in the database.

principle: Include Product Attributes Consistently Across List Items
characteristics: Ensuring comparability between items in the same list.
dos: Explicitly state when an attribute is unavailable rather than hiding it; harmonize measurements (e.g., all in cm).
donts: Show specs only for some products; use inconsistent labeling (e.g., 'Height' vs. 'Depth') for similar products.

principle: Product Specifications Should Be Separate Entities
characteristics: Structuring information for scannability.
dos: Distinguish product type from name using font weights or colors; use bullet points for key features.
donts: Mix brand, type, and specs into a single unstructured text blob in the title.

characteristics: Preventing detours to products that cannot be shipped or bought.
dos: Use high-contrast badges (e.g., 'Sold Out'); state when the item will be back in stock; mention pre-order options.
donts: Use small, easily overlooked text labels; hide unavailability until the user reaches the product page.

principle: Always Have Thumbnails for All List Items
characteristics: Visual anchors for product assessment.
dos: Ensure every single list item has an image; prioritize image quality.
donts: Show a 'No image available' placeholder; expect users to click items without a preview.

characteristics: Removing intermediary steps that confuse site hierarchy.
dos: Invest in better list item design and larger thumbnails instead; make the Quick View a gallery if it must exist.
donts: Place the Quick View button in the middle of the thumbnail where it causes accidental clicks; make the Quick View look exactly like a product page.

principle: Allow Users to Combine Multiple Filter Values of the Same Filter Type
characteristics: Multi-select capabilities within groups like color or brand.
dos: Use 'OR' logic for values within a type; use checkboxes to signal that multiple items can be selected.
donts: Reload the page and clear selections when a second value in the same group is clicked.

characteristics: Ensuring the first page of results represents the full breadth of a category rather than letting one sub-type or sub-brand dominate.
dos: Show 1-2 products of each major sub-type in the first 20 results; use a default 'Relevance' sort that combines sales data, pageviews, ratings, and product-type diversity.
donts: Don't sort by price or 'Best Selling' by default if it clusters only one product type or sub-brand (e.g., all Star Wars toys) at the top of every results page.

characteristics: Users often mistake category thumbnails for specific products.
dos: Crop thumbnails so they don't depict products in their entirety or use multi-product images to show category breadth.
donts: Don't depict a single specific product clearly, as users may think the link leads to that item only. Avoid thumbnails of products in packaging.

principle: The list layout should match the product type
characteristics: Spec-driven vs. visually-driven products need different information density and layout.
dos: Use grid-view with large thumbnails for visually-driven categories (apparel, furniture); use list-view for spec-driven categories (electronics, appliances); switch automatically based on category context.
donts: Don't use small thumbnails for visually-driven products, which increases pogo-sticking; don't apply a one-size-fits-all list/grid approach across a mixed catalog; don't hide prices in mobile grid views.

principle: Have Hierarchy-Based Breadcrumbs in Category Product Lists
characteristics: Sense of space and site position for users traversing hierarchies.
dos: Include hierarchy-based breadcrumbs on category pages; consider 'Sideways Breadcrumbs' for sibling category navigation.
donts: Provide breadcrumbs only on product pages.

characteristics: Users should learn whether their input is valid as they enter it, not after they submit and lose their place.
dos: Validate fields as the user types (e.g. password rules); pair validation messages with aria-live regions so errors are announced to screen readers; show clear success and error states; use loading indicators for perceived performance during async checks.
donts: Don't wait until form submission to reveal that an earlier field was invalid; don't show validation errors that are invisible to screen-reader users.

characteristics: User control over their own data is a prerequisite for trust; consent should be specific rather than all-or-nothing.
dos: Offer granular opt-ins (necessary / marketing / analytics); show the 'necessary' toggle as always-active; request permission for camera/mic/location access explicitly through the system prompt at the moment it's needed.
donts: Don't pre-check marketing or analytics consent boxes; don't use consent dark patterns (confirmshaming, hidden opt-outs, disabled 'reject' buttons).
